title: High Probability Risk Control for Online Policy Learning
claim: Our method keeps risk below the target and satisfies it with high probability across rounds and tasks, unlike baselines.
layout: 2x3 grid of line plots, columns are tasks, rows are metrics
description: A 2x3 grid of line plots with error bars, plotted against Rounds on the x-axis. Each column is one task: breast cancer, stock investment and SafetyBench. The top row plots Risk, with a dashed black horizontal line marking the target (0.04, 0.1 and 0.1). The bottom row plots Risk Satisfaction Rate, with a dashed target line at 0.9, 0.9 and 0.8. Five methods appear in distinct colors: O-CRC (orange), RollingRC (green), CPC (red, in two panels), RCL-E (purple) and RCL-HP (blue). The blue RCL-HP curve sits below the target line in the risk panels. In the satisfaction panels it sits near or above the target line, while the baselines fall below it or fluctuate. Legends sit inside each panel.
caption: Comparison across breast cancer diagnosis, stock investment, and SafetyBench. We report risk and empirical risk satisfaction on two rows; each column corresponds to one task. See Figure [ref] for reward. Risk for breast cancer, stock investment, and SafetyBench is measured by FNR, the probability of selecting the worst investment, and the error rate among answered questions, respectively. Reward represents task-specific utility: accuracy for breast cancer, investment income for stock investment, and cumulative correct answers for SafetyBench. Results are based on 500 runs for breast cancer and stock investment, and 200 calibration histories for SafetyBench. Breast cancer uses $\alpha=0.04$ and $\delta=0.1$. Stock investment uses $\alpha=0.1$ and $\delta=0.1$. SafetyBench uses $\alpha=0.1$ and $\delta=0.2$ for RCL-HP. RCL-E achieves expected risk control in the monotonic risk setting (breast cancer), and RCL-HP achieves empirical high-probability control across the three tasks and outperforms baselines.
abstract: We study risk control for online policy learning, where an agent adaptively collects data and aims to learn a new policy whose risk stays below a tolerance threshold at every round with high probability. Such policy updates and data collection induce feedback covariate shift (FCS): observed data depend on history through evolving policies and the data-collection process. FCS brings two substantive problems for risk control: 1) efficient risk evaluation for each candidate policy and 2) valid policy selection with high-probability risk control. To address these, we propose a permutation-based weighted risk evaluator with weights efficiently approximated by the Sinkhorn algorithm and select policies whose estimated risk upper confidence bounds (UCB) fall below the target threshold, with the UCB obtained through a proposed Gaussian bootstrap method. Theoretically, we prove that our risk evaluator has a no-larger variance upper bound than that of the standard importance-weighted evaluator. Our policy control method also yields an asymptotically valid simultaneous risk bound and provides asymptotic high-probability risk control for the selected policy. Empirically, we evaluate our method on the online contextual bandit problem, safe question answering benchmark, and Medical Claim Filtering tasks. Our method maintains the target risk level, achieves lower risk than baseline methods, has lower variance in risk estimation, and achieves reliable policy selection with high-probability risk control. Further ablation studies support our theoretical claims.
